summary: This bill requires the Secretary of Defense to publish and update every 90 days public lists of prohibited dietary supplement ingredients and performance-enhancing substances for Armed Forces members, allows commanding officers to waive discipline for first-time good-faith users in favor of education or counseling, and directs related DoD policy updates, website improvements, training reviews, and annual reports on enforcement.

scores.thoughts: The bill requires the Secretary of Defense to publish and update lists, maintain websites, produce reports, and incorporate education programs. These are minor administrative requirements with negligible spending implications and no provisions that expand or reduce overall government outlays.
The bill contains no provisions related to taxes, tax rates, deductions, or revenue collection.
While the bill addresses health-related supplements for service members, it does not engage with broader questions of public versus private healthcare systems or coverage models.
No provisions address firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
The bill has no connection to immigration policy, border enforcement, or pathways to citizenship.
No provisions relate to reproductive rights or abortion access.
The bill regulates conduct within the armed forces regarding supplements but does not alter military budgets, force structure, or defense spending levels.
No environmental, climate, or regulatory provisions are present.
The legislation does not address welfare programs, food assistance, or social safety-net policies.

The bill calls for limited education on supplement safety within existing military training programs, but this is narrowly scoped and does not affect public education funding, school choice, or federal education policy.

The bill creates and maintains lists of prohibited supplement ingredients for service members and distinguishes them from controlled substances under the CSA. It introduces limited discretion for first-time good-faith violations but does not alter general U.S. drug decriminalization or enforcement policy.

The bill allows commanding officers to forgo discipline or administrative separation for first-time good-faith possession/use of prohibited supplements. This introduces a modest element of leniency within the military justice context, but the change is narrow and does not address broader criminal justice reform or sentencing policy.
No trade, tariff, or globalization provisions appear in the bill.
The bill does not address deficits, debt reduction, or fiscal policy.
No provisions concern LGBTQ+ legal protections or rights.
The legislation contains no foreign aid or international assistance measures.
No voting, election integrity, or electoral reform provisions are included.
The bill directs minor website enhancements including AI label-scanning tools, but these are administrative features with no broader implications for technology regulation or data privacy policy.
The bill does not address worker protections, union rights, or employer flexibility.
No provisions involve religious exemptions or civil-rights balancing.
